questions.question: State the one law of formula writing, explain where ion charges come from, and use the law to build aluminium chloride and calcium oxide.
questions.expected_answer: The law: an ionic compound must be electrically neutral — total positive charge plus total negative charge must equal exactly zero, and the formula declares the ion ratio that achieves that zero. Charges are harvested from the periodic table and the data sheet's ion table: group one metals form one-plus ions, group two two-plus, aluminium three-plus; the halogens in group seventeen form one-minus ions, group sixteen two-minus, nitrogen three-minus. Aluminium chloride: Al three-plus against Cl one-minus — one or two chlorides cannot absorb plus three, but three can, so AlCl3, and the subscript is the arithmetic of neutrality made visible. Calcium oxide: Ca two-plus meets O two-minus — one of each cancels to zero, so CaO with no subscripts shown. Every formula is then verified by a charge audit that sums the charges back to zero.

questions.question: Perform the crossover for calcium chloride, state its two safety rules with examples, and explain why brackets are non-negotiable in ammonium sulphate.
questions.expected_answer: Crossover: write Ca two-plus and Cl one-minus side by side, take the size of each charge ignoring the sign, and cross diagonally — calcium's two becomes chlorine's subscript and chlorine's one becomes calcium's subscript, giving CaCl2. Safety rule one: simplify after crossing — calcium two-plus with oxide two-minus prints Ca2O2, but the two-to-two ratio is one-to-one in disguise, so the correct formula is CaO. Safety rule two: never write a subscript of one — CaCl2, not Ca1Cl2. Ammonium sulphate pairs NH4 one-plus with SO4 two-minus, needing two ammoniums per sulphate; when a polyatomic ion takes a subscript the whole team must be wrapped in brackets — (NH4)2SO4 — because without them NH42SO4 claims forty-two hydrogens and doubling the hydrogens by hand destroys the ion's identity. The bracket's subscript multiplies everything inside: two nitrogens and eight hydrogens, then one sulphur and four oxygens, and the charges audit to plus two against minus two — zero.

questions.question: Explain what the Roman numeral in iron(III) oxide means, derive the formula, contrast it with iron(II) oxide, and list the five steps of the complete method.
questions.expected_answer: Iron is a transition metal forming both Fe two-plus and Fe three-plus ions, so the name must announce which ion attended: the Roman numeral is the charge — iron(III) means Fe three-plus. Neutrality needs the lowest common multiple of three and two, which is six: two irons supply plus six and three oxides supply minus six, giving Fe2O3 — rust — which does not simplify because two and three share no factor. Iron(II) oxide is a different compound: Fe two-plus with O two-minus cancels one-for-one, giving FeO, black and different in colour, behaviour and mass — one numeral separates two substances. The five steps: one, name the two ions using the data sheet, Roman numerals and '-ate' endings; two, write both ions with their charges; three, find the neutral ratio by logic or crossover; four, simplify to the smallest ratio, bracket any multiplied polyatomic ion, and hide subscripts of one; five, audit — total plus cancels total minus and the atom count respects every bracket.
